title: The Unbelievers by Nick Payne at Manhattan Theatre Club #theunbelieve...
transcript: There's a moment in this play where two characters go in for a hug, but the energy is so lethal, you have to see it in context to understand why. In fact, almost everything the characters in this play say and do only makes sense in their unimaginable circumstances. The son of this nontraditional, blended family has been missing for days, months, or years, depending on the scene, and everyone has their own way of coping with it. Miriam is restless and relentless, never wavering on her commitment to track down her missing son, while David grieves the time that has been lost in the rabbit hole of grief itself. It is sad that we never get to see what this family looked like before this tragedy, but we can imagine based on the compassion they show one another in its aftermath. I honestly found myself getting frustrated with some of these characters and their behaviors, but of course, there are layers to their experience that I cannot relate to. It's easy to pass judgement as an outsider, and this play asks us to assume the best of people who are arguably at their worst. While I think it could benefit from some trimming, and I didn't get the idea behind ordering its scenes nonchronologically, The Unbelievers had me mostly on the edge of my seat with its compelling premise and even more compelling ensemble work.
